title: Assuming Equal String Tensions Across a Massive Accelerating Pulley
incorrect_statement: The tension in an ideal string remains uniform throughout its length even when passing over a real pulley with non-zero mass and moment of inertia.
why_it_fails: A massive pulley possesses rotational inertia I = 1/2 M R^2. By Newton's second law for rotation, an angular acceleration alpha requires a non-zero net external torque: tau_net = (T_1 - T_2) R = I alpha. If the string tensions on both sides were equal (T_1 = T_2), the net torque would be zero, making it physically impossible for the pulley to accelerate with the string without slipping.
diagnostic_symptom: Student sets T_1 = T_2 in Atwood machines or hanging mass problems with massive pulleys, resulting in an erroneous system acceleration.
corrective_explanation: Whenever a pulley has mass or moment of inertia, the tensions on either side of the pulley must differ: T_1 - T_2 = (I / R^2) a. Only in the idealized limit of a massless pulley (I -> 0) does T_1 = T_2.
supporting_evidence: University Physics, Chapter 10, Example 10.3; H.C. Verma Vol 1, Chapter 10, Section 10.8.
